strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and addresses a real gap: existing physical-plausibility evaluations for video generative models rely on subjective VLM/human judgments or trajectory matching, which the paper convincingly argues are prone to hallucination and false negatives. Evaluating conservation of physical invariants (energy, momentum, period) and fit to governing ODEs is a principled alternative.

The benchmark is grounded in real, controlled physical experiments (9 experiment types, 130 recordings, varied initial conditions) rather than synthetic/simulated data, and the gold-standard validation (real videos achieving Dynamical scores of 0.98–0.99 and Invariance scores >0.93) provides evidence the metrics behave as intended.

The evaluation scale is substantial: >9000 generated videos from six open-source VGMs (CogVideoX, PyramidalFlow, LTX-Video, Wan2.1, COSMOS-P1/P2) across single-frame, multi-frame, and keyframe conditioning, with useful analyses of discard failure modes (disappearance, duplication, stillness), prompt enhancement effects, and augmented-conditioning difficulty (Fig. 22).

The limitations discussion is unusually honest and thorough (Section 6 plus Appendix E), correctly identifying issues such as 2D-pixel ambiguity, neglected air resistance/friction, proxy nature of the scores, and short-horizon evaluation. Reproducibility is supported by released code and data, and the ethics and LLM-usage statements are appropriate.

The paper is careful to position keyframe-interpolation results (WAN-2.1, 0.55) as an easier interpolation task rather than treating them naively as evidence of superior extrapolative physical reasoning.
weaknesses: Several evaluation-protocol choices are ad hoc and potentially bias results. Most notably, different time-window sizes are used for real videos (L/10) vs. generated videos (L/4), which directly undermines the 'gold standard' comparison against the real-video upper bound; the authors themselves admit scores are 'highly sensitive to the choice of time window size'. The normalization constant α=1.0 is unjustified, and Eqs. 24/26 appear typographically identical, making the mean-near-zero fallback unclear.

The Dynamical score formula 'S_dyn = min(1 − NMSE, 0)' (App. D.3) appears to contain a sign error (presumably should be max), which raises concerns about the correctness or at least the care in the score implementation.

The discard mechanism conflates distinct failure modes with physical plausibility: 23–47% of generated videos are discarded and assigned a score of 0, so model rankings mix 'cannot track an object' with 'violates a conservation law'. The claim that discard criteria cleanly separate physical from non-physical videos rests on the heuristic SAM-2/DEVA/Grounded-SAM pipeline itself, whose error rates on generated (out-of-distribution) videos are not independently validated.

The physical assumptions are inconsistently applied: negligible-friction/no-air-resistance invariances (e.g., energy conservation) are used for rolling and sliding experiments where friction is central, which the authors acknowledge can 'penalize physically plausible generations' — an admitted evaluator mismatch that limits how much of the measured gap reflects model failure.

Per-video prompt conditions are cherry-picked at the model level ('we select the best scores between the enhanced and plain versions'), inflating headline scores relative to a fixed prompting protocol; this choice is not ablated.

Statistical rigor is thin: with only 10–22 recordings per experiment and no variance or significance analysis for model comparisons, differences between mid-ranked models (e.g., COSMOS-P2 at 0.43 vs. CogVideo at 0.32) are hard to interpret, especially given the visible per-experiment variability in Figs. 16–18.

The dataset is small and narrow (130 short clips, Newtonian mechanics only, static camera), Veo3/Veo3-fast were excluded mid-study for budget reasons yet their depth-consistency results still appear in Fig. 14, and Table 2's self-comparison presents the benchmark favorably without external validation that the new scores correlate better with human judgments of physical plausibility than existing metrics.

strengths: The core idea of grounding physical-plausibility evaluation in real, controlled laboratory experiments with known governing equations is a meaningful improvement over VLM-judgment or trajectory-matching evaluations, which can misclassify plausible generations.

The evaluation is fairly broad: 9 experiment types covering gravity, periodic motion, friction, and chaotic dynamics, ~9,000 generated videos across 6 open-source VGMs and three conditioning regimes, with useful fine-grained breakdowns (discard types, per-experiment heatmaps).

The decomposition into a discard rate, a PINN-based Dynamical score, and a Physical Invariance score gives an interpretable, quantitative framework, and validating metrics on real-world recordings as a 'gold standard' is a sensible sanity check.

Honest, substantive limitations section (App. E) that correctly identifies evaluator-mismatch risks (unmodeled friction/drag, 2D pixel trajectories, single-invariant insufficiency), and full code/data release supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The score design contains arbitrary and potentially validity-undermining choices that are not adequately justified. Taking the maximum score over sliding windows (App. D.5) rewards the 'best-looking' segment of a trajectory rather than overall physical consistency, and using different window sizes for real (L/10) vs. generated (L/4) videos makes the real-world 'upper bound' not directly comparable to model scores. The authors themselves admit scores are 'highly sensitive to the choice of time window size.'

The discard-rate metric conflates failure modes: up to 47% of videos are discarded and assigned zero Physical Invariance score, but discards are triggered by the pipeline's own segmentation/tracking (SAM-2, DEVA) and include 'stillness' — a physically valid (if degenerate) generation. Discarding then zero-scoring these videos systematically punishes models without measuring physics, and the paper provides no error analysis of the tracking pipeline itself.

The Dynamical score formulation is questionable. A PINN with a physics loss (λ=1) fit to a short, noisy trajectory can produce a low NMSE even when the underlying generation is unphysical (the PINN is itself pulled toward the governing ODE), and the reported formula Sdyn = min(1 − NMSE, 0) appears erroneous (as written it is ≤ 0 for any NMSE ≥ 0; presumably max was intended). This is a critical correctness issue in the central metric.

The assumed invariances (no air resistance, no friction, elastic collisions, negligible damping 'over a short period') violate the actual experimental setups (real pendulums have friction, sliding books have friction, bounces dissipate energy). The real-world videos themselves score only 0.86–0.87 on rolling and projectile (Fig. 8), showing evaluator mismatch rather than establishing a clean upper bound; the paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it.

No validation that the proposed scores correlate with human perception of physical plausibility or with known failure cases — the missing construct-validity check for a new benchmark metric. The qualitative examples (Fig. 15) hint at divergent scores (high Dynamical/low Invariance) but this discrepancy is never analyzed.

Scale and coverage are modest: only 130 real videos across 9 experiments, no camera calibration (2D pixel-space physics), static camera only, and Veo3 — cited as state of the art in the introduction — was dropped from the main analysis due to budget limits, so the 'current models struggle' claim rests on open-source models only.

Conditioning types are not compared on equal footing: WAN-2.1's best result uses keyframe interpolation with the final frame provided (an interpolation task), yet it is reported as the top model alongside extrapolation settings, muddying the headline ranking.

Presentation has multiple errors and rough edges ('comparsion', 'extarct', 'Reproducability', App. D.3 'The physics loss for free fall is defined as: The physics loss for free fall is defined as:', inconsistent 'non_holonomic' experiment appearing in results but not defined in the dataset description), which, together with the metric formula issue, suggests the work was not carefully checked.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated evaluation paradigm: instead of trajectory matching or VLM judgment, Morpheus scores generated videos against conservation laws and governing ODEs, which elegantly addresses the false-negative problem of trajectory matching when initial conditions are unobservable (Sec. 4, Fig. 1).

Carefully controlled real-world dataset: 9 experiments (falling, projectile, bouncing, pendulum, double pendulum, rolling, sliding, collision, spring) recorded under lab conditions with actuator-controlled release mechanisms and varied initial conditions, enabling targeted testing of specific physical laws rather than generic visual plausibility (Sec. 3, App. A).

Metrics are validated against real-world recordings used as a 'gold standard' (Dynamical scores 0.98-0.99, Invariance >0.93; Fig. 8), which establishes an upper bound and supports correctness of the experimental setups.

Extensive empirical study: >9000 generated videos across six open-source VGMs (CogVideoX, Cosmos-Predict1/2, Wan2.1, LTX-Video, PyramidalFlow) with three conditioning regimes (single frame, multi-frame, keyframe) and plain vs. enhanced prompting, yielding actionable findings (e.g., multi-frame conditioning helps; keyframe interpolation is an easier task than extrapolation).

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Sec. 6 and App. E), including admission that scores are proxies, sensitive to time-window choices, and that unmodeled forces (air drag, friction) can penalize plausible generations.
Good reproducibility commitment: full code on GitHub, data on Hugging Face, an open leaderboard, and detailed appendices on smoothing, PINN training, score scaling, and all prompts.
Thoughtful augmentation strategy (Cosmos-Transfer1 style transfer constrained by object masks) to diversify conditioning while preserving dynamics, with manual quality screening (App. B, Fig. 13).
weaknesses: Metric validity is asserted but not strongly demonstrated. The Physical Invariance score is essentially the standard deviation of a derived invariant over an arbitrarily chosen time window, with several hand-tuned workarounds (App. D.5: window of L/10 for real vs L/4 for generated videos, 'take the highest score across segments', a threshold rule when the mean invariant is near zero). These choices could systematically favor generated videos and are not validated against human judgment or known-good/bad examples.

The discard mechanism creates a composite metric of unclear semantics: discarded videos (up to 47% for some models) are assigned Invariance score 0, so overall scores conflate trajectory quality, object permanence, and physics adherence. The automatic discard filters (DEVA/Grounded-SAM based) are themselves error-prone, and no human audit of discard decisions on generated videos is reported.

Inconsistencies undermine trust in the reported evaluation scope: the introduction and abstract claim evaluation of models 'including Veo3', but App. D.2 admits Veo3/Veo3-fast were excluded from the final analysis due to budget limits (though Veo3 appears in the depth-consistency figure). The claim of being 'the first benchmark' to use physical laws is also overstated relative to VAMP and Physics-IQ-adjacent work that quantifies motion characteristics.

Small-scale evaluation: 130 real videos over 9 experiments, with 7-22 recordings each, limits statistical power; results are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, and per-cell counts in the model-by-experiment heatmaps (Figs. 16-21) are likely too small for the fine-grained conclusions drawn.

Pipeline noise is not characterized: velocity/acceleration are estimated from SAM2 masks plus a chain of smoothing steps (central difference, sliding-window regression with hand-set weight α=0.7, Savitzky-Golay). No error analysis of how tracking/smoothing errors propagate into the scores (e.g., how much of the real-video score of 0.846 for projectile vs 0.988 for pendulum reflects metric noise rather than physics).

The Dynamical score is somewhat opaque: the PINN is fit to the trajectory with the physics loss, and the score is an inverted NMSE 'vs. a worse-than-constant PINN fit', but details of the constant-fit baseline, PINN optimization stability across noisy short trajectories, and sensitivity to hyperparameters (λ=1, 200k iterations, tiny 2x20 network) are not analyzed.

Keyframe-interpolation results (Wan2.1 topping the leaderboard at 0.55) are not comparable to single/multi-frame extrapolation, as the authors themselves note, yet aggregate rankings mix these regimes without a clear separation in the headline figures.

Presentation issues: noticeable typos and grammatical errors ('extarct', 'comparsion', 'it's mass', 'worse-than-constant'), and some equations are stated loosely (e.g., S_dyn = min(1 - NMSE, 0), which is always 0 as written; Eq. 26 is identical to Eq. 24 with C_σ substituted for C_σ̄ without clear justification).

The benchmark is confined to short clips, static cameras, orthogonal 2D motion, and idealized physics (no friction/air resistance), so it measures a narrow slice of physical reasoning; the authors acknowledge this, but it reduces significance relative to the framing as evaluating 'world model' capability.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: a physics-informed evaluation framework (Morpheus) that assesses VGMs against governing ODEs and conserved quantities rather than subjective judgment or pixel-level trajectory matching, addressing a genuine gap in the literature (Table 2 comparison).

Careful metric validation: real-world videos serve as an upper bound (Dynamical 0.96–0.99, Invariance ≥ 0.90); the real-vs-real stress test (Table 7) convincingly shows trajectory matching penalizes valid physics; the VLM evaluator analysis (Tables 4–6) demonstrates that even a state-of-the-art physical-commonsense VLM hallucinates violations in clean real recordings, strongly motivating the framework.

Extensive robustness analyses: scale invariance (App. D.3), depth-consistency checks (App. D.4), PINN architecture ablation (Table 3), trajectory-noise perturbation (App. D.8), sliding-window ablation (Table 8), and human-alignment study (Spearman ρ = 0.708, App. D.10), plus validation of the discard filter against human majority vote (Fig. 19).

Broad model coverage (9 open- and closed-source VGMs, three conditioning regimes) with informative qualitative findings (keyframe conditioning dominance, stillness vs. duplication failure modes, context-dependent prompt-upsampler effects).

Honest, detailed limitations discussion (Sec. 6 and App. E) that correctly identifies evaluator-mismatch risks, 2D-ambiguity, and the proxy nature of the scores; data and code released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Narrow scope: 9 experiment categories with ~130 curated laboratory recordings under fixed, orthogonal cameras and short clips. The 'physical world modeling' conclusions are drawn from a small, idealized regime; generalization of the framework (and the negative findings) to natural, unconstrained video is untested.

Metric design contains ad hoc choices that could bias results: the Physical Invariance score is computed on the best-scoring 25% sliding window of each trajectory, and discarded videos are assigned a hard score of 0. The latter conflates outright generation failure with physical-law violation, so aggregated scores (Fig. 7) mix two qualitatively different failure modes; although ablations show rankings are stable, the absolute scores are hard to interpret.

The Physical Invariance score is uncorrelated with human judgment (ρ = −0.157), so its external validity rests mainly on the real-world reference; a single invariant looking 'good' does not preclude violations of other laws, which the authors acknowledge but do not quantify.

Discard filter recall is low (0.450), meaning many invalid videos pass through to physical scoring; while the authors argue the error direction is conservative, the effective sample of scored videos per model/experiment is small and unevenly filtered, raising variance concerns for model comparisons.

Assumptions such as negligible air resistance, perfect elasticity, and ideal Hookean springs are applied to both real and generated videos; deviations from these could penalize physically plausible generations (the authors argue real-world scores empirically bound this, but only for their specific setups).

Minor presentation/consistency issues: Table 3 reports the paper configuration score (e.g., pendulum 0.953) slightly above its own reported 'best' (0.95); some hyperparameter choices (λ, α=0.7, window sizes) are justified only empirically.

strengths: The core idea is sound and timely: evaluating video generative models at the level of governing ODEs and conserved invariants, rather than subjective VLM judgments or pixel-aligned trajectory matching, addresses a real gap in how 'world model' claims are tested.

The real-vs-real stress test (App. D.7) is a convincing argument that trajectory-matching metrics (Physics-IQ) penalize physically valid realizations, empirically motivating the framework rather than only asserting it.

The validation effort is substantial: real-world videos establish a near-ceiling reference (Dynamical 0.96–0.99, Invariance ≥ 0.90), and there are dedicated analyses of scale invariance, tracking noise (jitter/gaps), PINN architecture sensitivity, scoring-window length, depth consistency, and discard-filter false positives/negatives against human judgment.

The comparison against VideoPHY2-AUTOEVAL (App. D.6) is a valuable negative result: the state-of-the-art VLM judge assigns 0% JPC to many clean real-world recordings while rewarding generations of the same phenomena, directly supporting the paper's motivation.

Evaluation breadth is good: 9 models (closed- and open-source), three conditioning regimes (single/multi-frame, keyframe), and analysis of failure modes (stillness, duplication, disappearance) and per-experiment blind spots (pendulums, collisions).
The paper is generally honest about limitations (App. E is candid about 2D-pixel ambiguity, unmodeled dissipative forces, proxy nature of the scores, and short-clip scope).
weaknesses: Metric design choices raise soundness concerns. The Physical Invariance score is computed on the best-scoring 25% sliding window of each trajectory (App. D.12); this 'cherry-picks' the most stable segment and can systematically mask invariant violations. The window ablation (App. D.9) shows rankings are preserved, but absolute scores drop 0.05–0.10 under full-trajectory scoring, indicating the headline numbers depend on this choice.

Discarded trajectories are assigned a Physical Invariance score of 0 (Sec. 4.2), which conflates generation/tracking failure (stillness, duplication) with physics-law violation in the same headline metric, muddying what the aggregate score means.

The Physical Invariance score shows no correlation with human plausibility (ρ = −0.157, n.s., App. D.10) and is validated only against 'physics' via real-world ceiling scores. Given that the same smoothing pipeline is applied to real and generated videos, it remains unclear how discriminative and trustworthy this component is in isolation; the paper's defense (humans cannot see invariants) is plausible but leaves the score's construct validity under-supported.

Energy/invariant computations are performed in uncalibrated pixel units without camera calibration. While the Dynamical score is shown to be scale-invariant (App. D.3), the analogous check is not clearly established for invariance quantities that mix velocity-squared and position terms; rescaling or lens distortion could affect the invariance score differently than the PINN-based score.

The dataset is modest (≈130 recordings across 9 experiment types, some with only 7–12 videos, e.g., spring, bouncing) and all with a fixed, orthogonal, static camera; claims of a 'comprehensive evaluation' overstate the coverage, and the number of generations sampled per condition is not clearly reported, so confidence intervals or significance on the model rankings in Figs. 6–7 are absent.

The architecture ablation (Table 3) shows worst-case Dynamical scores as low as 0.09 (projectile) and 0.16 (pendulum), indicating the PINN fit is fragile for the more complex dynamics precisely where the benchmark is most interesting; λ hyperparameters and score-normalization choices add evaluator degrees of freedom despite the real-world-split tuning.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'it's mass', 'Our study does not any collection'), a somewhat self-serving Table 2 comparison ('first to use real physical laws'), and key methodology details relegated to a long appendix.

Scope limitation is acknowledged but material: with static cameras, short clips, and 2D pixel trajectories, the benchmark measures a narrow slice of 'Newtonian mechanics'; its relevance to the embodied-AI/robotics framing in the introduction is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper introduces Morpheus, a genuinely novel physics-informed evaluation framework that assesses video generative models against conservation laws and governing ODEs rather than subjective VLM judgments or pixel-level trajectory matching—a well-motivated and clearly positioned gap in the literature (Table 2 comparison).

The dataset is grounded in real, controlled physical experiments (9 experiment types, ~130 recordings with systematic variation of initial conditions), which is a meaningful advance over benchmarks built on simulated or uncontrolled in-the-wild video; the Cosmos-Transfer1 augmentation to diversify conditioning is a thoughtful addition.

Validation of the evaluation pipeline itself is unusually thorough: scale-invariance verification (App. D.3), depth-consistency checks justifying 2D trajectory analysis (App. D.4), PINN architecture ablation (App. D.5), robustness to tracking jitter/gaps (App. D.8), sliding-window ablation preserving rankings (App. D.9), discard-filter validation against human majority vote with a confusion matrix (Fig. 19), and human-alignment analysis (Spearman ρ=0.708, App. D.10).

The real-vs-real stress test against Physics-IQ trajectory matching (App. D.7) and the comparison against VideoPHY2-AUTOEVAL showing VLM evaluators fail on clean real-world physics (App. D.6) are convincing, well-designed experiments that substantiate the paper's central methodological claim.

The evaluation covers 9 state-of-the-art models across three conditioning regimes, and the analysis goes beyond rankings to identify interpretable failure modes (stillness, duplication, pendulum collapse) and conditioning effects (keyframe interpolation dominates; prompt upsampling is context-dependent).

The limitations discussion (Sec. 6 and App. E) is honest and substantive, correctly framing Morpheus as a focused stress test rather than a universal physics evaluator, and the impact statement addresses data/licensing concerns appropriately.
weaknesses: The scope of the benchmark is narrow: 9 rigid-body Newtonian experiment types, short clips, static orthogonal cameras, and idealized assumptions (negligible drag/friction/air resistance). While honestly acknowledged, this limits how broadly the headline conclusion ('models fail to encode physics') generalizes, and App. E concedes that a physically plausible generation can be penalized when idealized assumptions are violated.

Several metric design choices appear ad hoc and could benefit from stronger justification: the Physical Invariance score is computed on the best-scoring 25% sliding window (favoring the most stable segment), scores are assigned 0 for discarded trajectories (conflating generation failure with physical violation in aggregate scores), and λ weights (1 vs. 5) for the PINN physics loss are hand-set per experiment family (validated only on the real-world split).

The human-alignment result for the total score (ρ=0.708) is driven entirely by the dynamical score; the physical invariance score—the paper's most novel component—shows no significant correlation with human judgment (ρ=-0.157). The authors argue this is expected and validate invariance against physics instead, but it means the invariance score's discriminative validity rests mainly on the real-world ceiling (≥0.90) rather than independent behavioral validation.

The small human study (42 retained videos, 3 judges) and the discard-filter validation (65 videos) are modest in size; confidence intervals around per-model score differences (Figs. 7-8, 21-23) are not reported, making it hard to judge whether model rankings are statistically meaningful.

Conditioning regimes are asymmetric across models (only some support multi-frame or keyframe conditioning), so the 'open vs. closed source' and conditioning-level comparisons partially confound model capability with available conditioning interface.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('it's mass', 'Our study does not any collection', 'recoded' for 'recorded', 'a degrees angle'), Figure 8's per-experiment real-world scores are only in an appendix figure, and some invariant definitions are weak (e.g., sliding/rolling reduce to 'acceleration' constancy), limiting the sensitivity of the invariance score for those experiments.
